articles.title: Engaging in Ethical Activism by Healthcare Professionals: Ensuring Positive Impact without Alienation
articles.authors: White, Elysa; McKay, Dean; Feldman, Cassondra L.; Spence, Nicole Z.
articles.abstract: Abstract The politicization of healthcare has been a growing controversy. The current uptick in activism and advocacy, as well as other political acts, has made this controversy much more visible. Through a look at the rise in antisemitism in healthcare after 10/7, we examine how activism and other political acts can damage relationships of medical professionals and their colleagues and patients, which can undermine quality care. We urge further research and discussion on the role of activism and other overt political acts in healthcare and propose a framework to provide guidance.

articles.title: Weaponizing Trauma Theory against the Jews: A Rebuttal to “Antisemitism and the Unclaimed Past: A Trauma-Informed Critique of Jewish Political Discourse”
Antisemitism and the Unclaimed Past: A Trauma-Informed Critique of Jewish Political Discourse
articles.abstract: Abstract Since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, Jewish institutional life has intensified its vig­ilance toward antisemitism, often collapsing distinctions between antizionism, criticism of Israel, and genuine antisemitic threat. This article argues that such hypervigilance is not solely a strategic response to real danger, but also a collective trauma reflex rooted in centuries of persecution-from pogroms and the Holocaust to expulsions from Arab lands-now compounded by post-10/7 fears. Drawing on trauma theory, particularly Cathy Caruth’s concept of “unclaimed experience” and Bessel van der Kolk’s work on embodied trauma, alongside emerging epigenetic research, I examine how unprocessed historical suffering resurfaces in political discourse as policy, rhetoric, and defensive archi­tecture. Through news events, community events, and a close reading of the academic text Poisoning the Wells: Antisemitism in Contemporary America, I show how institutional nar­ratives often conflate dissent with danger, foreclosing critical differentiation and internal pluralism. I argue for a trauma-informed approach to antisemitism that honors the reality of the threats facing the Jewish community while also confronting the reality of inherited pain. The article proposes pathways for transforming fear-based reactions into ethically grounded, pluralistic, and courageous Jewish political engagement in a post-10/7 world.

articles.title: Antisemitic Narratives on Social Media Become More Radicalized: Increases in Posts Portraying Jews as Evil, Dehumanizing Jews, and from People Self-Identifying as Antisemitic since October 7, 2023
articles.authors: Leiba, Rotem; Lakshman, Srinidhi; Madnick, Harrison; Mulder, Steve
articles.abstract: Abstract This study examines the radicalization of antisemitic rhetoric on social media following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel. We analyzed English-language public posts from October 7, 2023, to July 28, 2025, and compared them with the preceding time period. Posts were categorized into three themes: depictions of Jews as inherently evil, de­humanizing language, and self-identification as antisemitic or aligned with Nazi ideology. Results show substantial increases across all categories-330%, 324%, and 250% respec­tively-indicating both quantitative and qualitative escalation. Particularly concerning is the rise in individuals openly embracing the label “antisemitic,” signaling an erosion of social stigma. These findings reflect a historical pattern in which normalization of hate facilitates radicalization, which can lead to real-world violence. The results underscore the urgent need for interventions to disrupt pathways from online antisemitic rhetoric to of­fline harm.

articles.title: Digital Radicalization and Campus Antisemitism: The Role of Social Media Networks in Mainstreaming Extremist Rhetoric
articles.abstract: Abstract Antizionist campus groups in the United States were active well before the Hamas mas­sacre on October 7, 2023, and the ensuing war in Gaza. However, they have increas­ingly moved to the center of public debate over the boundaries between pro-Palestinian activism, support for Hamas, and antisemitism. Drawing on a comprehensive dataset-including nearly 10,000 recorded antisemitic incidents across 571 universities, over 1,000 anti-Israel campus groups at 368 institutions, and more than 76,000 Instagram posts from 662 accounts-this study analyzes how digital coordination, radicalized rhetoric, and of­fline mobilization have converged on US campuses, particularly in the wake of October 7. It identifies the central actors behind a coordinated network of campus and off-campus groups whose messaging increasingly mirrors that of designated terrorist organizations, and shows that radicalized language once confined to the fringes-including the glorification of violence and the demonization of Israel-has since gained traction in mainstream online discourse. Key findings include: a strong statistical association between anti-Israel group presence and antisemitic incidents, especially pronounced on campuses already experienc­ing elevated incident rates; a surge in antisemitic incidents immediately following October 7 and a peak during the spring 2024 encampments; a significant intensification of online activity by campus groups after October 7, facilitated by Instagram’s co-authorship feature; and the emergence of a dense collaboration network linking local student organizations-above all SJP chapters-with radical off-campus groups and foreign ideological actors. These findings highlight the urgent need to understand and confront rising antisemitism and radicalization on US campuses.

articles.title: Thy Brother’s Keeper: Attributions of Blame and Responsibility in the Jewish and Muslim Diaspora
articles.abstract: Abstract Political violence, ranging from terrorism to interstate conflict, have been a core concern of social scientists for decades. Yet, the study of these phenomena and their effects is often limited to the specific geographic area of their occurrence. We seek to understand how diaspora populations and linked groups to international actors are affected by their geo­political actions. Namely, considered blameworthy for or responsible to speak out against the actions of states and/or transnational actors with whom they are often linked? We contend that the reporting of salient events associated with a particularly violent conflict, are likely to increase both blame and responsibility to speak out of groups associated with the perceived attacker. We test our hypotheses through three waves of survey experiments in the United States from 2022 to 2024. While support for our hypotheses is mixed, the clearest evidence for our expected effects appears only in the pre-conflict wave, prior to the October 7 attack and the subsequent war in Gaza. In the later wartime waves, these effects largely dissipate, suggesting that in a media environment already saturated with conflict reporting, exposure to a single additional conflict report may have limited marginal im­pact. More broadly, we find that blame and responsibility to speak function as distinct phenomenon targeting groups associated with international actors. Additionally, our work shows that those on the ideological right are much more likely to blame groups for the actions of associated international actors in conflict.

articles.title: Antisemitism in Higher Education in the United Kingdom: Jewish Students’ Experiences since October 7, 2023
articles.abstract: Abstract This study presents the findings of a comprehensive survey of Jewish students at UK uni­versities at the end of the 2023-2024 academic year (n = 497). Respondents reported witnessing many more antisemitic incidents after than before October 7. Furthermore, the greater the number of antisemitic incidents that students personally experienced and witnessed, the more people and spaces they avoided on campus due to antisemitism; the greater their concerns about antisemitism on campus; the more they felt unsafe on cam­pus; and the greater the negative effects of antisemitism on their studies, wellbeing and campus life. Students’ own words are highlighted in the open-ended responses, emphasiz­ing the verbal abuse, physical attacks, intimidation, exclusion, and isolation they experi­enced, hinting at profound negative effects on their mental health. Together, these findings underscore the pressing need to combat the surge in antisemitism across UK universities, for example, by creating and enforcing clear codes of conduct for staff and students to re­duce experiences and expressions of antisemitism, alongside robust reporting mechanisms to capture and address these when they do occur.

articles.title: Echoes of October 7: A Phenomenological Study of Jewish Students’ Experiences at a Small Liberal Arts College
articles.abstract: Abstract This article presents the results of phenomenological research on Jewish students’ experi­ences at a small liberal arts college (SLAC) in the aftermath of the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. Based on interviews with twenty-five students from diverse po­litical and religious backgrounds, it documents and analyzes student voices. The study dis­tinguishes common and differing themes in the narratives of pro-Israel and pro-Palestine positions the students expressed, and discusses the impact of campus events and activism, as well as the college’s responses, on the students’ Jewish identities.

articles.title: Virtue, Boycott, and Exclusion: Anthropology’s Turn against Israel
articles.abstract: Abstract This article offers a critical analysis of the American Anthropological Association’s (AAA) academic boycott of Israeli universities, combining institutional critique with an autoeth­nographic account of the author’s experience as an anthropologist opposing the boycott. It argues that this largest US academic boycott against Israel undermines academic freedom, weakens the AAA’s role as a forum for scholarly exchange, and contributes to professional polarization. The article contends that the boycott, though formally directed at institu­tions, inevitably harms individual scholars and disproportionately affects Israeli academics, including critics of their own government. It further suggests that the AAA’s alignment with broader BDS activism distorts scholarly norms, fosters ideological conformity, and creates a hostile environment for many Jewish anthropologists representing a troubling pattern in progressive academic circles. Drawing on debates within the AAA and broader academic trends, the essay concludes that academic boycotts are counterproductive, erode intellectual pluralism, and ultimately impede the pursuit of dialogue, understanding, and peace.

articles.title: Decolonial Psychology’s Blind Spot: From Liberation Praxis to Antisemitism
articles.authors: McKay, Dean; Bar-Halpern, Miri; Kogan, Jennifer; Hess, Susan; Yudell, Andrea
articles.abstract: Abstract Decolonial Therapy is a rapidly emerging treatment model promoted in the mental health professions. The approach is explicitly political, and has a foundation that readily fosters antisemitism. In this conceptual paper, the broad approach is described and its histori­cal antecedents laid out in the treatment model is actively harmful to Jewish clients and mental health professionals, creating a serious public health crisis. By explicitly demand­ing activism as part of treatment, psychological interventions have been transformed into political propaganda contexts in direct contrast with the expected clinical healing needs of the client. Decolonial aims could potentially involve empirical validation while retaining its focus on the needs of historically oppressed groups, including Jews. In the present manifestation of decolonial psychology, the framing of Jews as oppressors instead creates conditions for harm. The urgency of addressing the political and discriminatory nature of decolonial therapy has increased significantly since the attacks of October 7, 2023, as there are well-documented antisemitic incidents in the mental health professions that can be traced directly to the development of this treatment approach. The article concludes with recommendations for professional reform to overcome antisemitism in the mental health professions.

articles.title: From Insulation to Isolation: Why American Jewish Exceptionalism No Longer Protects Us from Antisemitism—and What Must Replace It
articles.abstract: Abstract This article argues that American Jewish exceptionalism, once a powerful narrative of safety, integration, and flourishing, has become a source of strategic and intellectual isolation in an era of resurgent antisemitism. For decades, the belief that the United States offered Jews a uniquely secure and pluralistic home helped structure communal institutions, academic priorities, and coalition politics. Yet that same narrative also fostered critical blind spots: it discouraged the development of formal expertise in antisemitism, treated antisemitism as episodic rather than structural, and encouraged Jewish participation in moral and political frameworks that often-rendered Jewish particularity unintelligible. The article traces how these dynamics have left American Jews and their institutions ill-prepared for a moment in which antisemitism has reentered mainstream discourse. It then examines the tensions involved in replacing this narrative, including debates over American exceptionalism, political polarization, Jewish intersectional identity, and the relationship between urgency and conceptual clarity. In response, the article proposes a structural path forward centered on building formal interdisciplinary expertise in Antisemitism Studies, prioritizing inter­vention research, and developing landscape mapping frameworks that can evaluate existing strategies, identify gaps, and promote accountability. Moving beyond symbolic reassurance and institutional inertia, the article calls for a new narrative grounded in evidence, resil­ience, and coordinated action.

Approaching Education in a Time of War: Aboutism and Virtuism at Jewish Summer Camps
articles.abstract: Abstract This study investigates how two North American Jewish overnight summer camps responded to the 2024 Israel–Gaza conflict by implementing distinct educational strategies proposed here as “ aboutism ” and “ virtuism .” At the Pennsylvania-based camp (PBC), the aboutism approach guided programming: Israeli-led expert sessions emphasized knowledge transmission about Israel’s geography, institutions, and conflict context. In contrast, at the Maryland-based camp (MBC), the virtuism approach prevailed: staff facilitated dialogue-based activities aimed at moral and identity development, valuing camper perspectives and peer discussion over structured fact-delivery. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork during the 2024 summer season, the analysis explores how each camp’s culture, staff composition, and perceptions of campers shaped these differing strategies. Findings show that while aboutism offered structured content and clarity, it limited opportunities for reflection and camper agency, and that virtuism promoted discussion and belonging, but often lacked shared foundational knowledge and concrete learning outcomes. The study argues that an integrated model—beginning with factual framing through aboutism, then transitioning to facilitator-led reflection via virtuism—could strengthen experiential learning in informal education contexts such as camps. These results contribute to understanding how informal, culture-rich settings can support experiential learning, identity formation, and cross-cultural dialogue.
